The Anatomy of a Rebel's Saddle: Mariano Matamoros
The Subject: Mariano Matamoros, a short, thin, pockmarked priest with a wandering eye, known
as Morelos's "left hand." He offered to "say masses or give saber strikes, interchangeably.
The Cigar Hole:
A custom hole carved into the
right side of the saddlehorn.
Why? To stick his lit cigar into
it during a cavalry charge. He
needed both hands free
(one for the reins, one for the
machete), couldn't keep it
in his mouth because the
smoke blinded him, and
refused to throw it away.
The Eaten Bridles:
During the brutal siege
of Cuautla, desperate and
starving after seven failed
charges, Matamoros
ordered his men to eat the
leather of their horse
bridles, gather their
strength, and charge again.
They broke the siege.

The bullets that couldn't find the target
Chihuahua hospital courtyard. Hidalgo complains about the milk in his final chocolate: "Just
because they are going to kill me doesn't mean they have to reduce my ration." He argues to
be shot facing forward and places his right hand over his heart as a target.
1. The First Volley:
Four soldiers fire from just four steps away. They all
miss the heart, hitting him only in the stomach. His
blindfold slips. He stares at them.
2. The Second Volley:
The second row fires. They shatter his stomach again.
The officer notes the soldiers are "trembling like
quicksilver." They are terrified of killing a priest.
3. The Point-Blank Finish:
The third row misses the heart again. Desperate, the
lieutenant orders two soldiers to place the muzzles of
their rifles directly against Hidalgo's heart to finally end it.

The Gatopardo: Why we must reject Agustin de Iturbide
The Myth: Modern revisionists attempt to paint Iturbide as a sensible liberator who avoided
further bloodshed.
THE BUTCHER: As a Royalist commander in the Baito,
he executed hundreds of guerillas without trial.
THE HOSTAGE TAKER: In 1814, he issued an edict
giving wives and daughters of insurgents 72 hours to
surrender. Over a hundred women were imprisoned for four
years; many died of disease or were violated.
THE WAR PROFITEER: He manipulated troop
movements to ensure his own mercury and cotton arrived first,
creating artificial scarcity to inflate prices for his personal profit.
THE HIJACKER: The Plan of Iguala was a conservative
coup to prevent social reform. The first government was
entirely composed of Royalist military, high clergy, and rich
Spaniards. He kidnapped the revolution.

Ten years in the iron cages of Guanajuato
The Warning (El Escarmiento):
By order of Brigadier Calleja, a local blacksmith named
Modesto Pérez forged four iron cages. The salted heads of
Hidalgo, Allende, Aldama, and Jiménez were hung on the
four corners of the Alhóndiga as a macabre trophy of the
counter-revolution. They rotted in the sun for ten years.
Divine Retribution:
While the executioner was caging the heads, an arrogant
Spanish loyalist kicked Hidalgo's cage, rolling the head
across the cobblestones. He triumphantly mounted his horse,
but the animal panicked, threw him to the ground, and
shattered his left leg. A wise old woman in the crowd
shouted: "God punishes without stick or stone."
